about: Black holes with a star going round them, found from the wobble Gaia measured in the star's path across the sky, then confirmed by the star's changing speed towards and away from us. None is feeding: nothing has been seen falling in, so they give off no light of their own. Each is found only by what it pulls on.
drawn: The star on its measured orbit at the clock's date. Both go round their shared centre of mass: the black hole, many times heavier, swings round a small loop of its own. The black hole's shadow is drawn at its true size, with the light from behind bent round it. The system stays where Gaia measured it (it really drifts across the sky, as the stars do, which aren't moved either).
about_fed: Black holes fed by the star going round them: gas from the star spirals into a disc round the black hole and heats up as it falls, the inner disc to millions of degrees, shining in X-rays. Some of it is flung out along the black hole's spin axis as jets, seen in radio.
drawn_fed: The star on its measured orbit at the clock's date, its shape the space where its own gravity rules (the black hole's pull stretches it), darker where its surface gravity is weaker. The disc at the temperatures disc theory gives for its measured feeding rate (V404 Cygni's: for the share of the light it gives), as the eye would see it up close, hotter and brighter on the side coming towards you, broken into the patches and rings its turbulence makes (the pattern ours: patches the size simulations give, each lasting about an orbit, carried round and sheared by the gas's motion, slowed to at most one inner orbit a second), its edges thinning out to see-through (ours: their profile isn't measured); its light, the star's and the sky's bent round the spinning black hole along the exact paths light takes there. The line marks the radio jet's direction; the jet itself isn't visible to the eye. The system stays where it was measured (it really drifts across the sky, as the stars do).

systems.name: Gaia BH1
systems.title: Dormant black hole with a Sun-like star
systems.about: Found in 2022 from the wobble of a Sun-like star in Gaia's measurements: then the nearest known black hole, three times closer than any other. The star swings round it on a wide oval, far too wide for the star's gas to spill onto it, so it isn't feeding: Chandra and the VLA saw no X-rays or radio from it.
refs: El-Badry et al. 2023, MNRAS 518, 1057 (Table 1: the joint Gaia + RV fit; RVs: their table)
Rodriguez et al. 2024, PASP 136, 024203 (no X-rays or radio)

systems.name: Gaia BH2
systems.title: Dormant black hole with a red giant
systems.about: Found in 2023, also from Gaia's measurements: a red giant (a star like the Sun near the end of its life, swollen to about 8 times its width) going round a black hole of about 9 Suns every 3.5 years. Even at its closest the giant is far too small to spill gas onto it, and no X-rays or radio were seen from it near its closest approach.
refs: El-Badry et al. 2023, MNRAS 521, 4323 (Table 2: the joint Gaia + RV fit; RVs: their Table 1)
Rodriguez et al. 2024, PASP 136, 024203 (no X-rays or radio)

systems.name: Gaia BH3
systems.title: Dormant black hole with an ancient giant
systems.about: Found in 2024 while checking data for Gaia's fourth release: about 33 Suns, then the most massive black hole of a star known in the Milky Way. Its star is one of the oldest kind, a giant with under 1/300 of the Sun's share of metals, from the halo: probably once in a small star cluster that the Milky Way tore apart (the ED-2 stream). They go round each other every 11.6 years on a long ellipse. Chandra saw no X-rays from it.
refs: Gaia Collaboration, Panuzzo et al. 2024, A&A 686, L2 (Table 2: the combined solution; Table 3: the star; RVs: Table C.1)
Cappelluti et al. 2024, ApJ 973, 75 (no X-rays)

systems.name: Cygnus X-1
systems.title: Black hole fed by a blue supergiant
systems.about: One of the first X-ray sources found (1964), and in 1972 the first object most astronomers accepted as a black hole, from the orbit of its star. The star, a blue supergiant 40 times the Sun's mass, nearly fills the space where its own gravity rules. The black hole draws in its fierce wind, which settles into a disc of gas millions of degrees hot, and it spins nearly as fast as anything can.
refs: Miller-Jones et al. 2021, Science 371, 1046 (distance 2.22 kpc; masses, orbit and star: Table 1; the orbit on the sky from VLBA astrometry: Tables S2, S3)
Zhao et al. 2021, ApJ 908, 117 (spin above 0.9985; the disc's feeding rate in the soft state, 1.8e17 g/s: Table 2)
Brocksopp et al. 1999, A&A 343, 861 (the ephemeris)

Smith, Heindl & Swank 2002, ApJ 569, 362 (no days-long viscous delays: the disc an order of magnitude smaller than an overflow-fed one, 'over a thousand gravitational radii'); El Mellah et al. 2019, A&A 622, A189 (a wind-captured disc much smaller than an overflow-fed one). Its outer edge, 3,000 rg, is our choice from these
Gaia DR3 (position, motion, G)

black_hole.spin_note: Zhao et al. 2021, at 3 sigma; drawn at 0.9985

systems.name: V404 Cygni
systems.title: Flaring black hole fed by a swollen orange star
systems.about: Flared in 1938 and again in 1989, when X-ray satellites caught it; in 1992 its star's orbit showed the dark companion had to be a black hole, the surest case then known. Its star, a little over half the Sun's mass and swollen to five times its width, fills the space where its gravity rules, and gas spills off its tip into a disc. Most of the time the disc is cool and faint and stops far short of the hole. Every few decades it floods inwards and the system flares (1938, 1989, 2015), briefly one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky. A third star goes round the pair at least 3,500 AU out.
refs: Casares et al. 2019, MNRAS 488, 1356 (period, T0, K2 and systemic velocity: Table 3)
Khargharia et al. 2010, ApJ 716, 1105 (black hole 9.0 +0.2/-0.6 Suns, inclination 67 +3/-1 deg; mass ratio 0.060 from Casares & Charles 1994)
Miller-Jones et al. 2009, ApJ 706, L230 (VLBI parallax and proper motion)
Gonzalez Hernandez et al. 2011, ApJ 738, 95 (the star: 4,800 K, [Fe/H] 0.20; the disc's 13% of the light at 640-660 nm, after Casares & Charles 1994)
Walton et al. 2017, ApJ 839, 110 (spin above 0.92)
Narayan, Barret & McClintock 1997, ApJ 482, 448; Shahbaz et al. 2003, MNRAS 346, 1116 (the quiet disc stops at ~10^4 Schwarzschild radii, a hot thin flow inside; its outer edge 2.3x10^5)
Miller-Jones et al. 2019, Nature 569, 374 (the jets' angle on the sky: -31 to +6 deg in 2015, swinging within hours; -16 deg quiet, from 1989)
Burdge et al. 2024, Nature 635, 316 (the third star)
Gaia DR3 (position, G)
